opening.headline: You will learn how coding agents differ from chatbots, where they spin, what they remember, and what they control when no one is present.
body: A coding agent is not a chatbot that creates a piece of code, but an agent that reads the code base, edits files, executes commands, and determines the next action based on the results. Configuration and control will vary depending on whether this agent is running on a terminal, cloud, or CI.

In this class, we will sequentially look at the configuration of Claude Code, cloud sessions that run even when the laptop is closed, headless execution for CI, integration with third-party providers, and memory files that pass instructions beyond the session. By matching it with Gemini CLI, we check the configuration shared by the two products and distinguish the control required when running from CI to headless.

As of 2026-10: General personal Google CLI access has transitioned to Antigravity CLI. The Gemini CLI command·GEMINI.md example below covers existing tools in Code Assist Standard·Enterprise or paid API key environments, which are still supported.

visual.alt: A scene where the demands of four people lead to different execution positions.
labels: I want to open a repository directly from the terminal
If the laptop continues to run even when closed
Automatic check in CI for each PR
Call only through our cloud provider

paragraphs: A team wants to introduce a coding agent. Developer A wants to open and use the repository directly from the terminal. Developer B wants the work to continue running even when the laptop is closed. The platform team wants to automatically run code checks on each pull request in CI. Security teams want to call models through the cloud providers their organization already uses.

All four demands point to the same “coding agent,” but where they are executed and how they are controlled. Even though it is the same product, the settings are completely different between running a terminal while talking to a person and running it in a CI without a person.

So what is the difference between a coding agent and a chatbot? The difference is that it has an agent loop that reads the codebase, modifies several files, executes commands, and then looks at the results and makes decisions. This class examines where and how the loop runs and what it remembers using Claude Code and Gemini CLI as examples.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can you meet the needs of all four people with one implementation? At the end of the lesson, you'll be able to pair the right practice for each need.

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: When using a code writing tool, have you ever had to repeat the same explanation from scratch every time?
items.answer: Starting with a new context for each conversation means you have to restate the rules and preferences of your project each time. To reduce this repetition, there is a device for passing instructions beyond the session, which is covered in this lesson as a memory file.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to turn around a long task and walk away to see its progress on another device?
items.answer: If the task is only running on my device, it stops the moment I close the device. If the session is running in the cloud instead of your device, it will continue even if you close the device and you can check the progress from any device.

items.prompt: Have you ever been in an unattended automated environment when a tool gets stuck asking for permission?
items.answer: Without people, work stops because no one can answer permission questions. In headless mode, which runs non-interactively, the tool to be used must be approved in advance to run until the end.

items.prompt: What questions will we answer in this class?
items.answer: It deals with where and how the coding agent moves, what it remembers, and what it controls when no one is present. Unlike chatbots, the focus is on the tool loop and execution environment.

screens.outro: First, let's take a look at what Claude Code is and where it circulates.

screens.title: Claude Code Overview: One Agent Loop, Multiple Surfaces
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what Claude Code is and where you can use it.

tabs.label: something
tabs.body: Claude Code is an AI coding assistant that understands your entire codebase and lets you implement features, fix bugs, and automate development tasks across multiple files and tools. Rather than simply creating a piece of code, it works as an agent loop that reads files, modifies them, executes commands, looks at the results, and decides the next action.

tabs.label: multiple surfaces
tabs.body: The same agent runs in the terminal, IDE extensions like VS Code and JetBrains, desktop apps, and the web. The surface may be different, but the loop is the same. The Terminal CLI lets you edit files, run commands, and manage projects from the command line. Which surface you choose is a matter of preference and work style.

tabs.label: Agent SDK
tabs.body: The Agent SDK allows you to use tools like Claude Code, agent loops, and context management as CLI, Python, or TypeScript packages. This means that I can call the coding agent's actions directly from my app or script. Headless execution is also a CLI form of this SDK.

tabs.label: Authentication method
tabs.body: Authentication methods vary depending on the surface. Use a subscription or console account, and the terminal and IDE also support third-party providers. When implementing it in your organization, you must first decide on which surfaces you will authenticate with which accounts and providers.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at the cloud session that continues to run even when the laptop is closed.

screens.title: Web and cloud environments: Sessions that continue running even when the laptop is closed
screens.lead: Select the “Cloud Session” and “Remote Control” buttons alternately to compare the differences between the two methods. Because their names are similar, they are often confused.

states.label: cloud session
states.body: Claude Code sessions run on cloud infrastructure instead of on your device. The default is infrastructure managed by Anthropic and can also be exported to your organization's self-hosted environment. It continues to spin even when you close your laptop, and you can check and change direction from any device. Start by going to your browser (claude.ai/code), the Code tab on the mobile app, selecting Cloud on the desktop app, `claude --cloud` in your terminal, and scheduling your cloud. All cloud sessions take place in a cloud environment. An environment is a saved configuration that determines network access, environment variables, secret values, and pre-startup setup scripts. The default environment only allows trusted network access, reaching only whitelisted domains such as package repositories. If you save the environment as a configuration, work will start under the same conditions for each session.

states.label: Remote Control
states.body: Remote control is a different feature from cloud sessions. I only control sessions running on my device from my phone or browser and do not use a cloud environment. So when my device is turned off, the session stops too. If you want your work to continue running even when you close your laptop, you should use a cloud session rather than remote control. The two methods have similar names, but the key point is that the location of the code is different.

screens.outro: Let's look at headless execution, which runs automatically without any human intervention.

screens.title: Headless execution and third-party integration
screens.lead: Please read the code alternately with the explanation on the right. This command checks CI for changes for each pull request.

data.code:
#Check PR changes without anyone
claude --bare -p "Find typos and dangerous patterns in this change and let me know" \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep" \
  --output-format json \
  --max-budget-usd 2.00 > review.json

#Pipeline branches with exit code
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "check failed"
  exit 1
fi

#Take out the result text and cost
jq -r '.result' review.json
jq '.total_cost_usd' review.json

notes.note: `-p` (`--print`) is a non-interactive mode that runs once and quits without any human input. `--bare` is CI-compliant as it produces the same results on any machine by skipping hooks, skills, MCP servers, memory, and automatic discovery of CLAUDE.md.

If you pre-authorize the tool you want to use with `--allowedTools`, it will run through to the end without asking permission. If you need a tool you haven't approved, in an unmanned environment, if there is no approval path, it will be rejected and your work will be blocked.
`--output-format json` provides structured results, session information, and costs. `stream-json` flows as a line-by-line event. `--max-budget-usd` is the upper bound on execution cost.
Exit code 0 on success, non-zero on failure, allowing the script to branch. Without this check, a failed check passes as if it succeeded.

With jq, take out the result text and `total_cost_usd` and write them as comments and cost logs. Third-party integrations allow organizations to deploy through providers such as Anthropic directly, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, and centrally handle authentication and routing with proxies and LLM gateways.

screens.outro: Next, we'll compare Gemini CLI and memory files, which carry instructions beyond the session.

screens.title: Memory files and Gemini CLI
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to see how the configurations of the two products correspond and how the instructions are delivered.

data.caption: Configuration comparison between Claude Code and Gemini CLI
rows: Write your coding standards, workflow, and project structure in CLAUDE.md. Auto Memories are notes that Claude writes directly after seeing your proofs and preferences.
The persistence context is given by the context file GEMINI.md.
Uses built-in tools such as file editing and command execution, as well as the MCP server.
It provides built-in tools such as file system, shell, and web import, as well as MCP server integration.
Run once with `claude -p` and you're done.
Limit the scope of execution to an environment isolated from permission settings.
Provides sandboxing to limit the scope of execution.
data.notes: Claude Code starts with a new context each session, and two devices - CLAUDE.md and automatic memory - carry the knowledge beyond the session. If you make the same mistake twice or enter the same correction over and over again, it's time to add it to your CLAUDE.md. Both are read as context and not enforced, so actions that need to be prevented must be prevented with a hook at all costs. Hooks are custom shell commands that Claude Code executes at set points in the lifecycle, regardless of whether the model attempts to follow the instructions. For example, if a PreToolUse hook that runs immediately before a tool call ends with exit code 2, that call is blocked, and a message written to standard error is passed as feedback to Claude. The difference is that CLAUDE.md is a context and a hook is code. The more specific and short the instructions are, the more likely they are to be followed. Gemini CLI is an open source agent that uses Gemini in the terminal.

screens.outro: Now that you have learned the concept, let's explain the example.

ext.title: Automate actions with hooks (Claude Code Docs)

screens.title: Commentary 1: Controls needed when running from CI to headless
screens.lead: The instructor will walk you through the controls needed to transition pull request inspection from CI to headless. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Each time a pull request is opened, the agent checks the changed diff and alerts you to typos and dangerous patterns. Since it runs automatically without human supervision, a control device must replace the human eye.

steps.title: permission
steps.body: Since there is no one, we only pre-approve read-centric tools with `--allowedTools` so that you don't get stuck on permission questions. Keeping writing or command execution tools open can cause inspection operations to change your code, so only allow the tools you need. Whitelisting is based on the principle of least privilege. Directives may be embedded in the pull request body or code comments that the agent reads (indirect prompt injection), and even if the model attempts to follow those instructions, the unauthorized tool will not run. Whitelisting is the first layer in scoping these risks, and isolated execution environments are the second layer.

steps.title: Reproducibility
steps.body: `--bare` eliminates the influence of personal settings and external MCP servers, ensuring the same results for all runners. Prevents hooks in a team member's home directory or the project's MCP settings from acting differently in CI.

steps.title: cost
steps.body: Put an upper limit of `--max-budget-usd` and log the cost field in the json output. Ensures costs remain predictable, even on PR-heavy days. Even if the task stops when the upper limit is reached, you should be able to check the log to see how much has been processed.

steps.title: Result processing
steps.body: Branch the pipeline with the exit code, and parse the json output into comments with jq. If the exit code is non-zero, the check failed and the pipeline should notice. This way, the point where people can check the results is naturally left as a comment in the pull request.

screens.outro: Next, we will summarize the criteria for classifying execution modes according to needs.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Different execution modes according to needs
screens.lead: As you select each need, the appropriate execution mode and reason will unfold. Try responding to the demands of the four people in the first scene one by one.

items.prompt: Need 1: I want to be able to touch local files with instant interaction.
items.answer: A terminal or IDE surface is suitable. You can directly connect to local files and change direction in the conversation while viewing the results. Developer A's request corresponds to this. This is the fastest way to view and edit files directly.

items.prompt: Request 2: I want to undo a long-running task and view it on another device.
items.answer: That's right, a cloud session. Because it runs on the cloud infrastructure, not my device, it continues to run even if I close the laptop. This is Developer B’s request. Remote controls do not fit this need as they stop when the device is turned off.

items.prompt: Request 3: I want to run it automatically and repeatedly without anyone.
items.answer: Headless (-p) or Agent SDK is correct. There are exit codes and structured output so scripts and CI can manipulate the results. This is a request from the platform team.

items.prompt: Requirement 4: Organizations must have a specific cloud provider agreement.
items.answer: The third-party provider configuration is correct. Models are called through providers, and authentication and routing can be centrally controlled through proxies and LLM gateways. This is what the security team needs.

items.prompt: Regardless of which mode you choose, what are the things you need to do in common?
items.answer: Leave your instructions in CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md so you don't have to explain them again every time. Even if the execution mode changes, the project's rules and preferences are read from the same file. Keep instructions specific and short.

screens.outro: Finally, let's distinguish what to write to the memory file.

screens.title: Commentary 3: What to write in the memory file
screens.lead: If you select a highlighted phrase in the CLAUDE.md example below, it will explain why the line is written that way and its limitations. The last line shows the difference between guidance and enforcement.

data.text:
# Project Guidelines
- The test is run with `npm test`.. The entire suite takes about 5 minutes, so only test the files that have been modified.
- API response type is Defined in `src/types/api.ts`. Do not arbitrarily create a new type.
- Perform First, tell us the plan in one line. before any code changes.
- Never modify the `migrations/` directory.

marks.span: The test is run with `npm test`.
marks.note: If this is the second time your agent has miswritten the test execution commands, it is time to write these short, specific facts into CLAUDE.md. Instead of typing the same corrections over and over again, write them down once. If the entire suite takes a long time, write that information down as well.
These are guidelines that give you a project structure that may be difficult to understand or take time to find even if you read the code. The more specific the route is, the better it is followed.

marks.span: First, tell us the plan in one line.
marks.note: Guidelines are to be read as context, not enforcement. To ensure consistency, keep it short and specific. Long and vague instructions make them less consistent to follow.
In any case, actions that must be prevented must be enforced with a hook, not just written down as guidelines. This line in CLAUDE.md is advisory, and the hook actually prevents the action.

screens.outro: Now, let's organize the concepts of this lesson into a map.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate the key concepts of this lesson. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

cards.back: One agent loop runs across the terminal, IDE, desktop app, and web surface. The Agent SDK allows you to use the same loop in your code.
Cloud sessions continue to run even when the laptop is closed. An environment is a saved configuration that specifies network access, environment variables, secret values, and setup scripts.
Non-interactive mode, run once with -p and quit. Set tool authorizations, output formats, cost caps, and branch to exit codes.
The model is invoked through the cloud provider and gateway used by the organization. Authentication and routing can be centrally controlled.
CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md contain instructions beyond the session. It's just a context, so if you need to force it, you use a hook.

screens.outro: Lastly, we will summarize the order in which you select the execution mode.

screens.title: How to choose an execution mode
screens.lead: The contents of this class are organized in the order in which they will be used in the coding agent introduction plan. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: When introducing a coding agent, first determine whether it is a task that needs to be watched by a person or a task that does not require human supervision. A terminal or IDE surface is suitable for observation and collaboration work, a cloud session is suitable for tasks that take a long time to be left, and headless execution is suitable for tasks that are repeated without human intervention.

Three controls must be in place for unmanned execution: These are the authority to pre-approve the tools to be used, reproducibility to produce the same results on any machine, and a cost cap. To this we add a branch that detects failures with exit codes.

At the organizational level, model call paths are controlled by third-party providers and gateways, and repeated descriptions are left in CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md. However, since the guidelines are only recommendations, actions that must be prevented are enforced by hook.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: A coding agent is a product that has one loop going around in multiple places. Where to turn is determined by whether people are watching, where to remain, and what to enforce.

glossary.def: It is a non-interactive mode that runs once and ends without human input with the -p flag.
This is a Claude Code session running on a cloud infrastructure, not on my device.
A Markdown file that records continuation instructions for a project, individual, or organization.
These are notes that Claude writes himself after looking at the user's corrections and preferences.
This is a user-defined script that the harness executes at a set point in time, and can operate regardless of the model's judgment, preventing or modifying tool calls.

misconceptions.myth: If written in CLAUDE.md, the rule is guaranteed to be followed.
misconceptions.fact: CLAUDE.md is only an instruction that is read into the context, not a force setting. Actions that must be prevented must be enforced with a hook.

misconceptions.myth: Remote control is a cloud session.
misconceptions.fact: Remote control is a function that allows you to control sessions running on your device from your phone or browser. It does not use a cloud environment, and sessions stop when the device is turned off.

misconceptions.myth: Headless also resolves permission questions on its own.
misconceptions.fact: If you don't pre-approve the tools you want to allow, the call may be rejected in an unmanned environment without an approval path. Set the tools to use with --allowedTools.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Coding Agent is a product that runs in a loop across terminals, IDEs, desktops, and web surfaces.
The cloud session continues to run even when the laptop is closed, and the configuration determines the network and secret values.
Headless execution aligns with CI with -p, tool pre-approval, structured output, and cost caps.
Organizations control model call paths to third-party providers and gateways.
CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are guidelines for reducing repetitive descriptions and use hooks when enforcement is required.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: What parts of my team's coding work do I need to be able to do without a human being and what do I absolutely need to do? How will the execution mode change accordingly?
